opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that not all domains are created equal. Some of them are what I'd call root nodes. If you get superintelligence in those, everything else kind of falls out downstream.

The clearest example to me is coding, or more broadly, autonomous software engineering. Software is the substrate through which an AI system interacts with the digital world. If you have a system that can write, debug, and maintain software at a superhuman level, it can build its own tools, run its own experiments, and improve its own training infrastructure. It becomes a general-purpose problem solver, because almost any task you care about on a computer can be reframed as a coding problem.

So when we started Reflection, the thesis was: don't try to boil the ocean and build superintelligence across every category at once. Pick the category that unlocks the rest. If you build a truly superhuman autonomous coding agent, you've effectively built the engine that can then go and solve the other categories, whether that's research, data analysis, or operating any piece of software a knowledge worker uses.

There's also a practical reason. Coding has really good properties for reinforcement learning. You often have verifiable signals: does the code run, do the tests pass, does the system behave correctly. That's exactly the kind of environment where we've historically seen superhuman performance emerge, if you think back to AlphaGo and AlphaZero, which a lot of us worked on or around. Those systems got superhuman because they had a clear reward signal and could practice at scale. Coding is the closest thing in the real world to that kind of environment that also has enormous economic value.

So "solved" is a bit of a provocative word, but what I mean is that once you crack superintelligence in those key categories, the remaining path to broader superintelligence becomes much more of an engineering and scaling problem than an open research question. The hard conceptual leap is behind you.

r001.rationale: The response says superhuman coding can unlock other categories and that the remaining path becomes an engineering and scaling problem, conveying that applying the capability further is operational.

r002.rationale: It mentions coding’s economic value, but does not frame pursuing another category as a decision about whether acquiring its data is worth the investment.

r003.rationale: It does not say earlier reinforcement-learning systems were not scaled further because doing so lacked sufficient economic justification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way we think about it at Reflection is that superintelligence isn't really one monolithic thing you either have or you don't. It's much more useful to think about it as a collection of capabilities in specific domains. And the reason I'd say the problem is "solved" once you have superintelligent systems in a particular category is that, in that category, you've crossed the threshold that actually matters: the system is doing the thing better than any human could, and it's doing it autonomously.

Take coding as the obvious example. If you have a system that can take a vague product goal, reason about the codebase, write and test the code, and iterate on it with less supervision and better results than the best engineers, then within software you've essentially achieved superintelligence. You don't need that same system to also be a world-class physicist or to write a novel for it to be transformative. The economic and scientific value is already there.

And the second part of why I think this framing is right is that the methods generalize. What made AlphaGo work was a recipe: a strong learned prior, plus reinforcement learning against a verifiable signal, plus search at inference time. Once you've shown that recipe produces superhuman performance in one domain, the question for the next domain is mostly an engineering question. Can you set up the environment, can you define the reward, can you scale the compute. It stops being a question of whether superintelligence is possible and becomes a question of where you point it next.

So I'd say the "problem" in the research sense is solved when you've demonstrated the full loop in a domain that matters. Everything after that is expanding the frontier category by category, and coding happens to be the one where the feedback signals are clean and the payoff is largest, because the system can then help build its own successors.

r001.rationale: The response says that demonstrating a recipe in one domain makes applying it to the next domain mostly an engineering question.

r002.rationale: It discusses economic value and payoff, but does not frame the next-category decision as whether acquiring the needed data is worth the investment.

r003.rationale: It does not say that earlier reinforcement-learning systems were not scaled further because the economics did not justify it.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between having a system that’s superhuman in a particular domain and having a system that can advance AI research itself. Being superhuman at chess doesn’t mean you’ve solved superintelligence. There’s still a lot of work required to get from that capability to a generally capable system.

But if you have a system that’s better than the best human researchers at developing AI—and it can actually run experiments, evaluate results, and improve the underlying methods—then you’ve automated the process that produces further progress. You haven’t necessarily built every capability yet, but you’ve built something that can do the work of getting there.

So “solved” in that sense means the remaining research can be carried out by the system. That’s still conditional on it being reliable across the whole research process, and it doesn’t mean deployment or safety is solved.

r001.rationale: The response says AI-research automation could carry out remaining research, but does not argue that superintelligence in particular categories establishes a recipe whose further application is operational.

r002.rationale: It does not frame pursuing another category as an economic decision or mention the cost or value of acquiring necessary data.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss earlier reinforcement-learning systems or attribute a decision not to scale them to insufficient economic justification.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between building a system that’s superhuman in a particular domain and building a system that can do the work of creating the next, more capable system. Being superhuman at chess doesn’t solve artificial superintelligence, because chess doesn’t give you a way to improve intelligence more generally.

But if you have a system that’s superhuman at AI research and engineering, that’s a different kind of capability. It can work on the algorithms, run experiments, and improve the systems themselves. At that point, you’ve automated the process that produces further advances in AI.

So I don’t mean that every capability appears immediately, or that there are no constraints left. You still need compute, you still need experiments, and those take time. I mean that the central intellectual bottleneck has been removed: you have a system that can drive the remaining progress itself.

r001.rationale: The response says superhuman AI research and engineering could drive further AI progress, but it does not argue that superintelligence in particular categories establishes a recipe whose further application is operational.

r002.rationale: It does not frame pursuing superintelligence in another category as an economic decision about whether acquiring data is worth the investment.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss earlier reinforcement-learning systems or attribute a decision not to scale them to insufficient economic justification.
